**Remark.** The statement calls $f \wedge g$ the "pointwise maximum", but defines it by $\min$; we prove the claim for the mapping as defined, i.e. the pointwise minimum.

**Lemma.** For all $a, b \in \R$: $\min\{a,b\} = \frac12\,(a + b - |a-b|)$.

*Proof.* Exactly one of $a \le b$ or $a > b$ holds.
- If $a \le b$: then $a - b \le 0$, so $|a-b| = -(a-b) = b - a$, and $\min\{a,b\} = a$. Hence $\frac12(a+b-|a-b|) = \frac12(a + b - b + a) = \frac12 \cdot 2a = a = \min\{a,b\}$.
- If $a > b$: then $a - b > 0$, so $|a-b| = a-b$, and $\min\{a,b\} = b$. Hence $\frac12(a+b-|a-b|) = \frac12(a+b-a+b) = \frac12\cdot 2b = b = \min\{a,b\}$. $\blacksquare$

**Proof of the theorem.** Both $f \wedge g$ and $h := \frac12(f+g-|f-g|)$ are mappings $S \to \R$, so they are equal iff they agree at every $s \in S$. Fix $s \in S$. By the definitions of pointwise addition, pointwise difference, absolute value of a real-valued function, and pointwise scalar multiplication,
$$h(s) = \tfrac12\big((f+g-|f-g|)(s)\big) = \tfrac12\big((f+g)(s) - |f-g|(s)\big) = \tfrac12\big(f(s)+g(s) - |f(s)-g(s)|\big).$$
(Here $f+g-|f-g|$ is the pointwise difference of $f+g$ and $|f-g|$.) Applying the Lemma with $a = f(s)$, $b = g(s)$ gives
$$h(s) = \min\{f(s), g(s)\} = (f\wedge g)(s).$$
Since $s \in S$ was arbitrary, $f \wedge g = \frac12(f+g-|f-g|)$. (If $S = \varnothing$ both are the empty mapping and the equality is trivial.) $\blacksquare$
